questions.q: What is the output of this counting sort code?
questions.code:

    result[x] += 1

questions.why: result[v] counts how many times v appears: 0 never, 1 three times, 2 once, 3 once. The list holds counts, not the sorted values.
questions.iq: Comparison Sorting: Quicksort usually has a running time of O(n log(n)), but is there an algorithm that can sort even faster? In general, this is not possible. Most sorting algorithms are comparison sorts, i.e., they sort a list just by comparing the elements to one another. A comparison sort algorithm cannot beat O(n log(n)) (worst-case) running time, since O(n log(n)) represents the minimum number of comparisons needed to know where to place each element. Alternative Sorting: Another sorting method, the counting sort, does not require comparison. Instead, you create an integer array whose index range covers the entire range of values in your array to sort. Each time a value occurs in the original array, you increment the counter at that index. At the end, run through your counting array, printing the value of each non-zero valued index that number of times. For example, consider an array arr = [1, 1, 3, 2, 1]. All of its values are in the range [0...3], so create an array of zeroes, result = [0, 0, 0, 0]. The results of each iteration follow: i arr[i] result 0 1 [0, 1, 0, 0] 1 1 [0, 2, 0, 0] 2 3 [0, 2, 0, 1] 3 2 [0, 2, 1, 1] 4 1 [0, 3, 1, 1] Now we can print the list of occurrences, 3 times 1, once 2 and once 3 or print the sorted array [1, 1, 1, 2, 3]. Given an array of integers, count and print the number of times each value appears as a list of space-separated integers in the order of the values (sorted ascending).

questions.q: Consonants must go at even indices and vowels at odd indices, each group keeping its original order. For input "abodec", what is the output?

questions.iq: Given a string, rearrange it such that the consonants occupy the even indices (0-based) and the vowels occupy the odd indices. The vowels and consonants should maintain their relative order from the original string. Return the rearranged string. Example 1: Input: betayu Output: btyeau Explanation: Here, the string is "betayu". We can rearrange the string as below: - Vowels in order: e, a, u - Consonants in order: b, t, y - Place consonants at even indices → b₀t₂y₄ - Place vowels at odd indices → b e t a y u Hence, btyeau is returned as the output. Example 2: Input: applee Output: papele Explanation: Here, the string is "applee". We can rearrange the string as below: - Vowels in order: a, e, e - Consonants in order: p, p, l - Place consonants at even indices → p₀p₂l₄ - Place vowels at odd indices → p a p e l e Hence, papele is returned as the output.

def longest(s):
    chars = set()
    left = best = 0
    for right in range(len(s)):
        while s[right] in chars:
            chars.remove(s[left])
            left += 1
        chars.add(s[right])

questions.q: Which statement best describes Agentic AI?
o: AI that answers one prompt and then waits for the next prompt
AI that plans steps, uses tools and takes actions toward a goal
AI that only classifies data into fixed, predefined categories
AI that is trained without any data from human sources
questions.why: Agentic AI pursues a goal by planning, choosing actions and using tools with limited human input; a single prompt-response is ordinary (non-agentic) AI.
questions.iq: What is Agentic AI?

questions.q: Why is n8n commonly used?

To host and serve static HTML websites on the internet
To connect apps and automate multi-step workflows using nodes
To design user interfaces and export them as code

questions.q: Which example shows agentic behaviour?

An assistant that searches flights, compares fares, books and reports

questions.iq: Explain Agentic AI.

questions.q: What is the typical working loop of an AI agent?

Receive goal -> act with a tool -> stop without checking the result
Train model -> deploy model -> answer a single question -> stop
Observe result -> receive goal -> plan -> retrain the model
questions.why: Agents run a loop: plan, act (often via tools), observe the outcome and decide the next step until the goal is met.
questions.iq: How will AI agents work?

questions.q: A company offers an 'agentic AI service' for customer support. What makes it different from a basic FAQ chatbot?
o: It replies faster because it uses shorter canned answers
It can take actions in connected systems, like checking orders or issuing refunds
It only works on a website and never on mobile apps
It answers questions without using any AI model at all
questions.why: An agentic service connects to tools/systems and completes tasks end to end, not just returns text.
questions.iq: What is Agentic AI Service?

questions.q: What is the role of an orchestrator in an AI agent system?
o: It stores the model weights and trains them every night
It converts user text into tokens for the model
It coordinates which agent or tool runs when and passes outputs between steps
It renders the final answer as HTML for the browser
questions.why: The orchestrator manages the flow: routing tasks to agents/tools, ordering steps and handing results along.
questions.iq: What is the role of an orchestrator in AI agents?

questions.q: In an n8n workflow, what does a trigger node do?
o: It formats the final output before it is sent
It stores all workflow data permanently in a database
It stops the workflow when an error happens
It starts the workflow when an event occurs, like a schedule or webhook call

A button that changes the app theme from light to dark
A static list of productivity tips shown on the home page
A form that saves tasks to the database when submitted

questions.q: Which set of components together make up a typical AI agent?
o: A training dataset, a GPU and a loss function only
An LLM, tools it can call, memory and goal instructions
A frontend, a CSS framework and a static database
A prompt, a temperature value and a token limit only
questions.why: An agent wraps an LLM (reasoning) with tools (actions), memory (context) and instructions (goal/rules).

o: With a webhook, your app keeps requesting the server every few seconds
Webhooks work only for GET requests, polling only for POST
With a webhook, the source sends an HTTP request to your URL when the event occurs
Webhooks need the user to refresh the page to get new data

questions.q: An LLM agent is asked, 'Will it rain in Hyderabad tomorrow?' The LLM itself has no live data. What does a well-built agent do?

Refuse, since LLMs can never answer questions about the weather
Ask the user to search the weather and paste the result
Call a weather API tool, read the result, then answer

questions.q: What is the key difference between a standard AI model response and Agentic AI?

Standard AI can use tools, but agentic AI can only generate text
Agentic AI always gives shorter answers than standard AI

questions.q: In an event analytics platform, an email-open event arrives 3 days after it happened. How should the near-real-time dashboard handle it?

questions.iq: **Scenario:** A multi-tenant platform captures user interaction events such as page views, button clicks, form submissions, email opens, and application status changes. Currently, events are available in a data lake with a 24-hour delay and analytics are batch-only. The goal is to build an event-driven analytics platform that supports near-real-time dashboards while continuing to support existing batch analytics. **Key Requirements:** 1. **High Event Volume:** Handle up to 50,000 events/second at peak across 500+ tenants. 2. **Multiple Event Sources:** Collect events from browser JS SDKs, mobile applications, backend services, and third-party webhooks such as email provider callbacks. 3. **Schema Evolution:** Support new event types and additional fields without breaking existing consumers or downstream systems. Use backward-compatible schema evolution/versioning. 4. **Late-Arriving Events:** Handle events that arrive hours or days later, such as an email open tracked 3 days after sending. Real-time dashboards should support retroactive corrections when late events arrive. 5. **Tenant Data Isolation:** Ensure strict tenant-level data isolation so one tenant can never access another tenant's data, including aggregated views. Isolation should be enforced at the data/query layer, not only at the application layer. 6. **Real-Time + Batch Analytics:** Support sub-minute latency for real-time dashboards while maintaining historical data for monthly trends, cohort analysis, and other batch analytics. **Guiding Questions:** * How would you handle schema evolution without breaking downstream consumers? * How would you handle late-arriving events and update real-time dashboard metrics? * Where would you enforce tenant isolation — ingestion, storage, query time, or multiple layers — and why? * How would you design the architecture to support both real-time and batch analytics?

questions.q: What is an HTTP status code?
o: A unique number the browser assigns to every web page it opens
A three-digit number the server sends back to show the result of a request
The IP address of the server that hosts the website
A code written inside HTML to change how a page looks
questions.why: Every HTTP response carries a three-digit status code (like 200 or 404) that tells the client whether the request succeeded, failed, or needs another action. It is not an address or an HTML feature.
questions.iq: What are HTTP status codes?

questions.q: What is the main difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
o: HTTPS encrypts data between browser and server using TLS/SSL; HTTP sends it as plain text
HTTP is used for images and HTTPS is used only for text content
HTTPS works only on mobile browsers while HTTP works on desktops
HTTPS loads pages faster because it skips the DNS lookup step
questions.why: HTTPS is HTTP over a TLS-encrypted connection, so data like passwords cannot be read in transit. It does not skip DNS or depend on device or content type.
questions.iq: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?

questions.q: What is web hosting?
o: Writing the HTML and CSS code that makes up a website
Installing a web browser on a computer to open websites
Storing a website's files on a server connected to the internet so users can access it
Registering a domain name such as mysite.com with a registrar
questions.why: A hosting provider keeps your site's files on an always-on server that responds to visitors' requests. Buying a domain name is a separate step that only gives the site a human-readable address.
questions.iq: What is web hosting?

questions.q: What is an HTTP request?
o: A file stored on the server that lists all website visitors
A message the server sends to the browser containing the final web page
A message a client sends to a server asking for a resource or an action
A setting in the browser that decides which websites are allowed
questions.why: The client (browser or app) sends an HTTP request, e.g. GET /index.html, and the server replies with an HTTP response. Mixing up request and response is a common mistake.
questions.iq: What are HTTP requests?

questions.q: Which part of an HTTP request tells the server what action the client wants to perform, such as reading or creating data?
o: The status code, such as 200 or 404
The response body sent back by the server
The domain name, such as example.com
The HTTP method, such as GET or POST
questions.why: The method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.) states the intended action. Status codes belong to responses, not requests.
questions.iq: What is an HTTP request?

questions.q: An API returns a status code that starts with 4 (like 400, 401, 404). What does the 4xx range indicate?
o: The resource has moved and the client should be redirected
A server-side error, such as the server crashing
A client-side error, such as a bad request or missing permission
The request was successful and data was returned
questions.why: 4xx codes mean the problem lies with the request sent by the client. Server failures use 5xx, success uses 2xx, and redirects use 3xx.
questions.iq: What are API status codes?

questions.q: What is the main job of DNS (Domain Name System)?
o: Speeding up pages by compressing images before sending
Translating domain names like google.com into IP addresses
Storing a website's HTML, CSS and image files
Encrypting data sent between the browser and the server
questions.why: Computers locate servers by IP address, so DNS acts like the internet's phonebook and converts human-friendly names into IPs. Encryption is done by TLS and file storage by hosting servers.
questions.iq: What is DNS (Domain Name System)?

questions.q: What does HTTP status code 400 mean?
o: Unauthorized: the client must log in before accessing the resource
Internal Server Error: the server crashed while handling the request
Bad Request: the server cannot process the request because it is malformed or invalid
Not Found: the requested page does not exist on the server
questions.why: 400 Bad Request means the request itself is wrong, such as invalid JSON or missing required fields. 404 is Not Found, 401 is Unauthorized and 500 is a server error.
questions.iq: What does HTTP status code 400 mean?

questions.q: A user visits example.com/abouts (a typo) and the page does not exist. Which status code will the server most likely return?
questions.why: 404 means the server is reachable but the requested resource does not exist. It is a client-side error, not a server crash (500).
questions.iq: What does HTTP status code 404 mean?

questions.q: Which of the following status codes indicates that a request was successful?
questions.why: 200 OK means the request succeeded. 404 (Not Found) and 401 (Unauthorized) are client errors, and 500 is a server error.
questions.iq: What are the common HTTP status codes?

questions.q: An app sends hundreds of requests per minute to an API and starts receiving status code 429. What does this mean?
o: Service Unavailable: the server is down for maintenance
Request Timeout: the server took too long to respond
Too Many Requests: the client has hit the API's rate limit
Not Found: the API endpoint does not exist
questions.why: 429 Too Many Requests is returned when a client exceeds the allowed request rate; it should slow down and retry later. Timeouts and downtime have different codes (408, 503).
questions.iq: What does the HTTP status code 429 mean?

questions.q: What does HTTP status code 304 Not Modified mean?
o: The resource has not changed, so the browser can use its cached copy
The client is not allowed to modify this resource
The server failed to update the resource due to an error
The resource was deleted from the server permanently
questions.why: 304 is a redirection-class response telling the browser its cached version is still valid, saving bandwidth. It is not about permissions or failures.
questions.iq: What does the HTTP status code 304 mean?

questions.q: What does HTTP status code 200 indicate?
o: Accepted: the request was received but not yet processed
Redirect: the resource is available at a different URL
OK: the request succeeded and the server returned the expected response
Created: a new resource was created on the server
questions.why: 200 OK is the standard success response. 201 means Created, 202 means Accepted, and 3xx codes are redirects.
questions.iq: What does HTTP status code 200 indicate?

questions.q: What does the 403 Forbidden status code mean?

The client has not logged in and must provide valid credentials first
The server understood the request but refuses access because the client lacks permission
The server encountered an unexpected internal error
questions.why: 403 means access is denied even though the request was understood. A missing or invalid login is 401 Unauthorized, which students often confuse with 403.
questions.iq: What does the 403 Forbidden status code mean?

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes status codes 200 and 400?
o: 200 means the page was not found; 400 means the server crashed
200 means the request was invalid; 400 means the request succeeded
200 means a redirect happened; 400 means access is forbidden
200 means the request succeeded; 400 means the request was invalid
questions.why: 200 OK signals success, while 400 Bad Request signals a malformed or invalid client request.
questions.iq: What do the HTTP status codes 200 and 400 mean?

questions.q: What are the HTTP status codes for 'Created' and 'OK' respectively?
questions.why: 201 Created confirms a new resource was made (usually after POST), and 200 OK is the generic success code. 204 means No Content and 202 means Accepted.
questions.iq: What are the HTTP status codes for 'Created' and 'OK'?

questions.q: When you type www.example.com for the first time, in what order is the IP address typically looked up?
o: Authoritative server -> TLD server -> root server -> recursive resolver -> OS cache -> browser cache
Root server -> browser cache -> authoritative server -> TLD server -> OS cache -> recursive resolver

Recursive resolver -> authoritative server -> browser cache -> root server -> TLD server -> OS cache
questions.why: Local caches are checked first; if they miss, the recursive resolver walks the hierarchy from root to TLD (.com) to the domain's authoritative server.
questions.iq: How does DNS work?

questions.q: During DNS resolution of www.example.com, which server holds the actual record with the site's IP address?
questions.why: Root and TLD servers only point the resolver to the next server; the authoritative nameserver for the domain stores the actual A record.
questions.iq: How does DNS resolution work?

questions.q: A recursive resolver asks the .com TLD server about www.example.com. What does the TLD server return?
o: An error, because TLD servers only handle email domains
The address of the authoritative nameserver for example.com
The final IP address of www.example.com
The HTML content of the example.com homepage
questions.why: TLD servers do not store individual site IPs; they refer the resolver to the domain's authoritative nameserver. Assuming the TLD returns the final IP is a common misconception.
questions.iq: How does the DNS system work?

questions.q: In a DNS query, what is the role of the recursive resolver (often run by your ISP or a provider like 8.8.8.8)?
o: It queries root, TLD and authoritative servers on the client's behalf and returns the final IP
It stores the website's files and sends them to the browser
It encrypts the connection between browser and web server
It permanently owns and edits the DNS records of every domain
questions.why: The resolver does the legwork of following referrals through the DNS hierarchy and caches the answer. Domain owners manage records on authoritative servers, not resolvers.
questions.iq: What is DNS and how does a DNS query work?

questions.q: What is the usual way a frontend connects to a backend in a web application?
o: By sharing the same CSS file between frontend and backend
By copying all backend code into the HTML file before deployment
By opening the backend's database file directly inside the browser
By sending HTTP requests to backend API endpoints and receiving data, usually as JSON
questions.why: The frontend and backend communicate over HTTP via APIs, which keeps them independent and keeps the database secure on the server.
questions.iq: How do you connect the frontend and backend?

questions.q: A React frontend is deployed on Vercel and an Express backend on Render. The deployed site loads, but no data appears even though it worked locally. What is the most likely fix?
o: Move the database inside the React build folder
Update the frontend's API base URL from localhost to the deployed backend URL
Change every API call in the frontend from GET to DELETE
Rename all frontend files to .php so the backend can read them
questions.why: After deployment, localhost refers to the user's own machine, so the frontend must call the backend's public URL (usually set via an environment variable).
questions.iq: How can you deploy the frontend and backend?

questions.q: Before a browser sends an HTTP request, it opens a TCP connection with the server. What is the correct order of the TCP three-way handshake?
questions.why: The client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client confirms with ACK. Only then is the connection ready for HTTP data.
questions.iq: How does the client-server connection happen?

questions.q: On the backend, what is the typical lifecycle of a request?
o: Middleware checks auth -> response sent -> request received -> route handler runs logic
Request received -> middleware (parse body, check auth) -> route handler runs logic/DB query -> response sent with status code
Response sent with status code -> request received -> middleware runs -> route handler runs logic
Route handler runs logic -> request received -> response sent -> middleware checks auth
questions.why: Middleware prepares and checks the request before the matching route handler does the work, and the cycle ends when a response is sent back.
questions.iq: Explain the backend request-response lifecycle.

questions.q: You type www.nxtwave.com in the browser and press Enter. If the IP is not cached anywhere, what must happen first?
o: The browser renders the page layout using CSS
A DNS lookup to find the server's IP address
The browser runs the page's JavaScript files
The server sends the HTML page to the browser
questions.why: The browser cannot contact the server without its IP address, so DNS resolution comes before connecting, requesting, receiving or rendering anything.
questions.iq: What happens when you type a URL in the browser?

questions.q: A frontend needs to update only the email of user 42 through a REST API. Which request is most appropriate?
o: DELETE /api/users/42 with the new email in the body
PATCH /api/users/42 with the new email in the JSON body
questions.why: PATCH applies a partial update to a resource identified by its URL. GET should not change data, and DELETE removes the resource.
questions.iq: How does a REST API connect the frontend and backend?

questions.q: Computers communicate using IP addresses. Why is DNS still needed to access websites?
o: DNS stores the website's pages so they load without contacting a server
IP addresses only work for email, so websites need domain names
Names are easier to remember, and the site's IP can change without users needing a new address
Without DNS, data between browser and server would not be encrypted
questions.why: DNS maps memorable names to IPs and lets owners move servers by just updating records. Encryption (TLS) and content storage (hosting) are unrelated to DNS.
questions.iq: What is DNS, and how does it help in accessing websites?

questions.q: A frontend at http://localhost:3000 calls a backend at http://localhost:5000, and the browser console shows a CORS error. What is the correct fix?
o: Add more CSS to the frontend so the browser trusts the page
Configure the backend to send an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header allowing the frontend's origin
Change the frontend's request method from GET to POST
Return status code 404 from the backend for cross-origin requests
questions.why: Different ports are different origins, so the browser blocks the response unless the server explicitly allows that origin via CORS headers.
questions.iq: How do you connect the frontend and backend in a project?

questions.q: A client sends GET /api/products/7. In a client-server architecture, what does /api/products/7 represent?
o: An endpoint URL identifying the specific product resource with id 7
The status code the server will return for the request
The IP address of the server hosting the API
The name of the database table the browser will open directly
questions.why: An endpoint is the path that identifies a resource on the server, while the method (GET) says what to do with it. The server, not the browser, talks to the database.
questions.iq: How do API endpoints work in a client-server architecture?

questions.q: A website moves to a new server and updates its DNS record, but some users still reach the old server for a few hours. Why?
o: DNS servers only update records once a week on Sundays
The users' browsers have permanently blocked the new IP
The new server returned a 404 status code for those users
Resolvers and browsers have cached the old record until its TTL (time to live) expires
questions.why: DNS answers are cached for the duration set by the record's TTL, so changes take time to spread across the internet.
questions.iq: What is DNS (Domain Name System) and how does it function?

questions.q: When a browser needs to resolve a domain name to an IP address, where does it look first?
o: Its own DNS cache from earlier visits
The authoritative nameserver of the domain
questions.why: Checking local caches first avoids network lookups. Only on a cache miss does the query go out to resolvers and the DNS hierarchy.
questions.iq: How does a browser resolve a domain name to an IP address?

questions.q: A browser sends an HTTPS request to a web server across the internet. Which pair identifies the server machine and the service on it by default?
o: The browser's IP address and port 80
The server's MAC address and port 3306
The server's IP address and port 443
The server's domain name and port 21
questions.why: Packets are routed to the destination IP, and HTTPS uses port 443 by default (HTTP uses 80). MAC addresses only matter within the local network.
questions.iq: How does an HTTP request travel from the user to the server?

questions.q: What is the difference between HTTP status codes 401 and 403?
o: 401 means the user is not authenticated; 403 means the user is known but lacks permission
401 means the page was not found; 403 means the server crashed
401 means the request succeeded; 403 means the request was redirected
401 means the user lacks permission; 403 means the user is not authenticated
questions.why: 401 Unauthorized asks for valid credentials, whereas 403 Forbidden denies access even with a valid identity. Their names make swapping them a frequent mistake.
questions.iq: What is the difference between HTTP status codes 401 and 403?

questions.q: An API returns 400 for one request and 500 for another. Which interpretation is correct?
o: Both mean the server is down and the client should wait
400 means the client must fix its request; 500 means something failed on the server
400 means the server failed; 500 means the client sent bad data
400 means success with warnings; 500 means success with no data
questions.why: 4xx codes blame the request (fix the input and retry), while 5xx codes indicate a server-side fault the client usually cannot fix.
questions.iq: Can you explain common HTTP status codes such as 400 and 500?

questions.q: What should replace ___ so this frontend code sends the form data to the backend as JSON?
questions.code:
<script>
    fetch("/api/login", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        body: ___
    });
</script>
questions.why: The request body must be a string, so the object is converted with JSON.stringify. JSON.parse does the opposite (string to object), and passing a raw object sends '[object Object]'.
questions.iq: How do you connect the frontend and backend of an application?

questions.q: The backend sends a JSON response to the frontend's fetch() call. What must the frontend do before using fields like data.name?
o: Send the response back to the server for decoding
Parse the response body, for example with await response.json()
Convert the response into CSS using response.css()
Nothing, because fetch() returns plain JavaScript objects automatically
questions.why: fetch() resolves to a Response object; its body must be parsed with response.json() to get a usable JavaScript object.
questions.iq: How do you connect the frontend and backend in a web application?

questions.q: After the browser gets the server's IP address from DNS, what happens next?
o: The server sends a 200 OK response immediately
The browser renders the page using the HTML
The browser establishes a TCP connection with the server
The browser runs a second DNS lookup for the same domain
questions.why: With the IP known, the browser opens a TCP connection (plus TLS for HTTPS) before sending the HTTP request. Rendering only happens after a response arrives.
questions.iq: What happens when you enter a URL in the browser and press Enter?

questions.q: You are testing GET /api/users/999, where user 999 does not exist. Which assertion is most appropriate?
o: Status code is 200 and the body is always empty
Status code is 500 because the user is missing
Status code is 404 and the body contains a clear error message
Status code is 201 because the server created the user
questions.why: A missing resource should produce 404 with a helpful message. A 500 would wrongly signal a server crash, and 200 hides the error.
questions.iq: How would you validate API responses/status codes during testing?

questions.q: Which statement correctly explains the 2xx, 3xx and 5xx status code classes?
questions.why: The first digit gives the class: 2 success, 3 redirection, 4 client error, 5 server error.
questions.iq: Explain the significance of 200, 300, and 500 status codes in APIs.

questions.q: What does the first digit of an HTTP status code tell you?
o: The category of the response, such as success, redirection or error
The version of HTTP used by the browser
The number of times the request was retried
How many seconds the server took to respond
questions.why: Status codes are grouped by first digit: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
questions.iq: What are the different HTTP status codes and what do they indicate?

questions.q: A recursive resolver has no cached data for www.example.com. Which server does it contact first?
questions.why: Without cached hints, the resolver starts at the top of the hierarchy (root), which points it to the .com TLD, which points to the authoritative server.
questions.iq: What is DNS and how does it work? Explain the DNS resolution process.

questions.q: A login API receives a request whose JSON body is missing the required 'password' field entirely. Which status code is most appropriate?
questions.why: A structurally incomplete request is a 400. 401 fits when the request is well-formed but the credentials are wrong or absent from auth, and 500 would wrongly blame the server.
questions.iq: Explain the significance of HTTP status codes like 200, 400, and 401.

questions.q: Which DNS record type maps a domain name to an IPv4 address?
questions.why: An A record stores the IPv4 address. MX points to mail servers, CNAME aliases one name to another, and TXT holds text data.
questions.iq: What is DNS (Domain Name System) and how does it function in networking?

questions.q: What does the fetch() function in JavaScript (used in React apps) return when it is called?
o: A Promise that resolves to a Response object
The HTTP status code as a number
An HTML element containing the server's reply
questions.why: fetch() is asynchronous and returns a Promise; once resolved, you get a Response object whose body you can read with .json() or .text().
questions.iq: What is the fetch API in React, and how is it used to make HTTP requests?

questions.q: What is the basic difference between GET and POST requests?
o: GET is used only for images; POST is used only for HTML pages
GET sends data in the request body; POST sends data only in the URL
GET encrypts the data; POST sends the data as plain text
GET retrieves data and sends parameters in the URL; POST sends data in the request body, often to create something
questions.why: GET is meant for reading and puts parameters in the query string, while POST carries a body for submitting data. Neither method itself encrypts data; HTTPS does.
questions.iq: What is the basic difference between GET and POST methods in HTTP requests?

questions.q: You run a traceroute (tracert) from your laptop to a web server. What information does it show?
o: The HTML source code of the web server's homepage
Each intermediate router (hop) on the path and the time taken to reach it
The list of HTTP status codes the server has returned
All the cookies the web server has stored in your browser
questions.why: Traceroute reveals the network path hop by hop with latency, helping locate where delays or failures happen. It does not deal with HTTP content.
questions.iq: How do you trace the path of a packet from a user's browser to a web server?

questions.q: You open https://example.com. After the TCP connection is established, what extra step happens before the HTTP request is sent?
o: A second DNS lookup for the HTTPS version
The server sends a 301 redirect to HTTP
A TLS handshake to set up encryption
The browser renders a cached copy of the page
questions.why: HTTPS requires a TLS handshake (certificate check and key exchange) after TCP connects, so the HTTP request is sent encrypted.
questions.iq: What happens internally when you enter a URL in the browser and press Enter?

questions.q: During DNS resolution, a resolver asks a root nameserver for www.example.com. What does the root server return?
o: A 404 status code because root servers store no domains
The authoritative nameserver's copy of the site's HTML
A referral to the nameservers for the .com TLD
questions.why: Root servers only know where each TLD's nameservers are, so they refer the resolver onward. The actual IP comes later from the authoritative server.
questions.iq: How does the Domain Name System (DNS) resolve a domain name to an IP address?

questions.q: A DELETE /api/posts/15 request succeeds and the server has nothing to send back in the body. Which status code fits best?
questions.why: 204 indicates success with an intentionally empty body, which is common for DELETE. 201 is for creation, and 404 would mean the post did not exist.
questions.iq: Which status codes are used for different API request and response scenarios?

questions.q: A user enters a URL they visited a few minutes ago, and the IP is still in the OS DNS cache. What happens during the DNS lookup?
o: The browser must still contact the root server first
The cached IP is ignored and a new domain is registered
The cached IP is used and no query goes to external DNS servers
The browser asks the web server itself for its IP address
questions.why: Cached answers that have not expired (TTL) are reused, skipping the network lookup and making the page load faster.
questions.iq: What happens during a DNS lookup when a user enters a website URL in the browser?

questions.q: The HTML page received by Chrome links to style.css, app.js and logo.png. How does the browser get these files?
o: It sends separate HTTP requests for each file while parsing the HTML
The browser downloads them from the DNS server
They are always included inside the original HTML response
The server pushes them only after the user scrolls the page
questions.why: As the browser parses HTML and finds linked resources, it requests each one, then uses them to build and render the page.
questions.iq: What happens when you enter a URL in Google Chrome? Explain the complete process.

questions.q: A user who is not logged in calls GET /api/orders, which requires authentication. Which status code should the API return?
questions.why: No valid credentials were provided, so 401 tells the client to authenticate. 403 is for authenticated users who still lack permission.
questions.iq: Explain commonly used HTTP status codes (e.g., 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 500).

questions.q: How do APIs allow a frontend team and a backend team to work independently?
o: The API is an agreed contract of endpoints, request formats and responses, so each side only depends on that contract
The API copies the backend source code into the frontend project
The API lets the frontend read the backend's database tables directly
The API removes the need for HTTP when both teams use the same language
questions.why: As long as both sides honour the API contract, the frontend need not know how the backend is built internally, and vice versa.
questions.iq: What are APIs, and how do they facilitate communication between frontend and backend?

questions.q: In a frontend-backend request/response flow, where does middleware such as an authentication check run?
o: In the database, after the query results are saved
In the DNS server, before the IP address is returned
In the browser, after the response has been rendered
On the server, after the request arrives and before the route handler runs
questions.why: Middleware sits in the server's pipeline between receiving the request and the final handler, so it can log, parse, or block requests early.
questions.iq: How do you integrate middleware between the frontend and backend request/response flow?

questions.q: A FastAPI application is ready to serve requests. Which server is commonly used to run it?
o: Apache Tomcat, a Java servlet container
questions.why: FastAPI is an ASGI framework, so it needs an ASGI server like Uvicorn to accept HTTP connections. npm and pip only install packages.
questions.iq: Do you have knowledge of FastAPI? What web server is used with FastAPI, such as Uvicorn?

questions.q: What does Express.js mainly add on top of Node.js's built-in http module?
o: Simple routing (app.get, app.post) and middleware support for handling requests
A built-in database that replaces MongoDB and MySQL
A visual editor for designing HTML pages
Automatic DNS registration for the server's domain
questions.why: With the raw http module you manually parse URLs and methods; Express provides clean route methods and a middleware chain, making servers faster to build.
questions.iq: What is Express.js? How does it simplify the process of building a web server in Node.js?

questions.q: What happens with this code if the server responds with status 500?
questions.code:
<script>
    async function loadData() {
        try {
            const response = await fetch("/api/data");
            console.log("Got response");
        } catch (error) {
            console.log("Request failed");
        }
    }
</script>
o: fetch() returns undefined and the program stops immediately
The catch block runs automatically because 500 is an error
The catch block does not run; the code must check response.ok or the status itself
The browser retries the request until it gets status 200
questions.why: fetch() only rejects on network-level failures; any HTTP response, including 404 or 500, resolves normally. So you need both a status check and try-catch.
questions.iq: Why can't you depend solely on the backend response status codes instead of using try-catch?

questions.q: What is the correct order of steps when a JWT is used for authentication?
o: Client creates a JWT -> server stores it in the database -> user logs in -> server signs it
User logs in -> server verifies credentials and signs a JWT -> client stores it -> client sends it with each request -> server verifies it
Server sends a JWT to every visitor -> user logs in -> client deletes token -> server re-checks password each time
Client sends JWT with request -> user logs in -> server signs JWT -> client stores it
questions.why: The server issues a signed token only after verifying credentials; the client then attaches it (usually in the Authorization header) to later requests.
questions.iq: Describe the process of how a JWT is used for authentication in a client-server interaction.

questions.q: A frontend calls an API and receives 401 Unauthorized because the user's session has ended. What is the best way to handle it?
o: Redirect the user to the login page (or refresh the token) and then retry
Keep resending the same request in a loop until it returns 200
Show a 'Server is down' message and ask the user to wait
Ignore the response and show the old data as if nothing happened
questions.why: 401 means credentials are missing or invalid, so re-authenticating is the fix. Blind retries will keep failing, and it is not a server outage.
questions.iq: Explain the HTTP methods and status codes used in APIs. How do you handle errors in API responses?

questions.q: You fixed a bug in your backend code on your laptop, but the live website still shows the bug. What is the most likely reason?
o: The updated code has not been pushed and redeployed to the hosting server
The DNS server is still running the old backend code
The browser cannot display changes made to backend code
Backend bugs can only be fixed by changing the domain name
questions.why: The live site runs whatever version is deployed on the host, so changes must be committed, pushed and redeployed before users see them.
questions.iq: How can you make changes to the frontend and backend code after the application has been published?

questions.q: How does a server typically verify a JWT sent with a request?
o: It looks up the token's IP address in the DNS records
It checks the token's signature with its secret key and confirms the token has not expired
It decrypts the user's password stored inside the token and compares it
It asks the client's browser to confirm the token is genuine
questions.why: A JWT is signed, so the server can validate its integrity and expiry without storing sessions. Passwords should never be placed inside a JWT.
questions.iq: Describe the step-by-step process of how JWT is used for authentication in a client-server architecture.

questions.q: In Express.js, a middleware function logs each request but neither calls next() nor sends a response. What happens to incoming requests?
o: Express automatically skips to the route handler
They hang without a response until the client times out
The server immediately returns 200 OK with an empty body
Express restarts the server to clear the request
questions.why: Middleware must either end the cycle (e.g. res.send) or pass control with next(); otherwise the request is stuck in the pipeline.
questions.iq: How do you handle HTTP requests and responses in Express.js? Explain the use of middleware in Express.js.

questions.q: A backend API works fine when tested in Postman, but calling it from a frontend on another domain fails with a CORS error. Why?
o: The API returns different data to browsers than to Postman
The frontend domain is missing an A record in DNS
Postman uses a different HTTP version that the server prefers
CORS is enforced by the browser, and the server has not allowed the frontend's origin
questions.why: CORS is a browser security policy; tools like Postman do not apply it. The server must include headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin for the frontend's origin.
questions.iq: What is CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing), and how does it relate to web security between the frontend and backend?

questions.q: In a Spring Boot API, a request asks for a user ID that does not exist. Which response is the best practice?
o: Return 200 OK with the text 'error' in the body
Return 500 Internal Server Error with an empty body
Return 201 Created with an empty user object
Return 404 Not Found with a JSON body like {"message": "User not found"}
questions.why: The status code should reflect the real outcome so clients can handle it, and a clear message helps debugging. Sending 200 for errors is a common mistake.
questions.iq: Handle API success and failure responses in a Spring Boot application, ensuring proper error messages and status codes are returned.

questions.q: A client sends a request with an expired auth token to a protected endpoint. Which status code should the API return?
questions.why: An expired token means the client is no longer authenticated, so 401 tells it to re-authenticate. 403 is for valid users without permission.
questions.iq: Q13. A client sends a request with an expired auth token to a protected endpoint. Which status code should the API correctly return?

questions.q: What is the correct order of the complete web request flow?
o: TCP connection -> DNS lookup -> page rendering -> HTTP request -> server processing -> HTTP response
HTTP request -> DNS lookup -> server processing -> TCP connection -> page rendering -> HTTP response
DNS lookup -> HTTP request -> TCP connection -> HTTP response -> server processing -> page rendering
DNS lookup -> TCP connection -> HTTP request -> server processing -> HTTP response -> page rendering
questions.why: The browser needs the IP (DNS) to connect (TCP), must connect before sending the request, and can render only after the server processes and responds.
questions.iq: Explain the complete request flow, including DNS lookup, TCP/HTTP connection, request processing, server response, and page rendering.

questions.q: A script posts a message to a Telegram group using the Telegram Bot API. Which request is correct?
o: POST https://telegram.org/login with the group admin's password
GET https://api.telegram.org/sendMessage with only the message text
questions.why: The Bot API authenticates using the secret bot token in the URL path, and sendMessage needs chat_id and text. Without the token the request cannot be authorised.
questions.iq: Describe the process of sending HTTP requests to the Telegram Bot API to post messages to a group. What authentication mechanisms are involved?

questions.q: Which statement best describes the 'stateless' principle of REST APIs?
o: The frontend and backend must be written in the same language
The server stores every client's previous requests and reuses them
Each request must carry all the information needed, since the server keeps no client session between requests
The API never changes any data stored in the database
questions.why: Statelessness means requests are independent (e.g. a token is sent each time), which makes REST APIs easier to scale. It does not forbid changing data.
questions.iq: REST Architecture & Principles: What are the key architectural principles of REST APIs (e.g., statelessness, client-server separation, uniform interface)?

questions.q: A test for an API that returns LLM responses only checks that the status code is 200. Why is this not enough?
o: Only 201 is a valid success code for LLM APIs
A 200 response can still be too slow or miss expected fields, so time and body content must be checked too
Status codes are never sent by APIs that return AI-generated text
A 200 status code always means the server crashed
questions.why: Status code, response time and the presence of expected fields are all part of a good API test; 200 only proves the request was handled.
questions.iq: You are testing an API that returns LLM responses. Which should be verified? A) Response status code B) Response time C) Presence of expected fields D) All of the above

questions.q: This code fetches Instagram posts. In which situation will the catch block definitely run?
questions.code:
<script>
    async function getPosts() {
        try {
            const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/posts");
            const data = await res.json();
            console.log(data);
        } catch (err) {
            console.log("Something went wrong");
        }
    }
</script>
o: The user's internet is disconnected, so no response reaches the browser
The API returns 200 with an empty posts array
The API returns 401 with a JSON error because the token is invalid
The API returns 404 with a JSON error because the account does not exist
questions.why: Network failures produce no HTTP response, so fetch() rejects and only try-catch can handle it. HTTP error responses with valid JSON still resolve and must be checked via the status.
questions.iq: Suppose we are fetching Instagram posts via an API. The API returns a status code (e.g., 200) and an array of posts or an error message. Why do we still need try-catch if the API clearly communicates errors?

questions.q: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH requests?
o: PUT sends data in the URL; PATCH cannot send any data
PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH updates only the fields that are sent
PUT only reads data; PATCH only deletes data
PUT deletes the resource; PATCH creates a new resource
questions.why: PUT sends a full representation that replaces the existing one, while PATCH applies a partial change. Both send data in the request body.
questions.iq: HTTP Methods & Status Codes: Explain the differences between standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) and give examples of common HTTP response status codes (e.g., 200, 201, 400, 401, 404, 500).

questions.q: A user clicks 'Checkout' and nothing happens. In the browser's Network tab, no request appears when the button is clicked. What is the most likely cause?
o: The click event listener is not attached, or a JavaScript error stops the code before the API call
The payment API is responding slowly due to high traffic
The backend returned 500 Internal Server Error
The user's auth token expired and the API returned 401
questions.why: If no request is sent at all, the problem is on the frontend before the API call. Status codes like 500 or 401 or a slow API would only matter if a request had actually been made.
questions.iq: If a user clicks on the "Checkout" button in an e-commerce flow and nothing happens (no response, spinner, or error message), how would you debug the issue? Follow-ups: How would you verify token authorization headers, API failure status codes, event listener attachments, and state management issues?

questions.q: In a MERN-style project (MongoDB, Express, React, Node.js), which option correctly assigns each layer's role?
o: MongoDB builds the UI, React handles APIs, Express stores the data
React builds the UI, Express/Node handle APIs, MongoDB stores the data
Node.js styles the pages, MongoDB routes requests, React stores data
Express builds the UI, MongoDB handles APIs, React stores the data
questions.why: React is the frontend, Express on Node.js is the backend API layer, and MongoDB is the database that persists data.
questions.iq: How did you build the frontend and backend?

questions.q: An ESP32 connected to home Wi-Fi runs a small web server on port 80. How can you open its page from a phone on the same Wi-Fi?
o: Type the Wi-Fi password into the browser's address bar
Open the phone's settings and enable the ESP32's DNS server
Search for 'ESP32' on Google to find its page
Type the ESP32's local IP address, such as http://192.168.1.50, in the phone's browser
questions.why: A device web server is reached by its IP address on the network; port 80 is the HTTP default so it need not be typed. Search engines do not index private local devices.
questions.iq: How did you create a web server on the ESP32?

questions.q: A React frontend calls POST /api/product, but the Express backend only defines app.post('/api/products', ...). What will the frontend most likely receive?
questions.why: The path does not match any defined route, so Express responds with 404. Mismatched paths or methods are a very common integration bug.
questions.iq: How did you connect the frontend and backend?

questions.q: Which endpoint follows REST conventions to fetch all orders of user 7?
questions.why: REST uses nouns for resources in the URL and the HTTP method for the action, so GET on /users/7/orders reads that collection. Verbs in URLs break the convention.
questions.iq: How did you connect the frontend and backend using REST APIs?

questions.q: In a full-stack project, where must input validation (e.g. checking email format) definitely be done for security?
o: In the CSS file, using input styles
On the backend, because frontend checks can be bypassed
Only on the frontend, because the backend never sees the input
In the DNS records of the website
questions.why: Frontend validation improves user experience, but anyone can send requests directly to the API, so the backend must validate too.
questions.iq: Did you work on both the frontend and backend of the project?

questions.q: A team builds the frontend in React. Why might they choose Node.js with Express for the backend?
o: The whole stack uses JavaScript, so the same language and JSON fit both sides
Node.js stores data permanently without needing any database
Node.js is the only backend that can send HTTP responses
React apps cannot connect to backends written in other languages
questions.why: Using JavaScript end to end simplifies development and knowledge sharing. React can talk to any backend over HTTP, so Node is a choice, not a requirement.
questions.iq: What technologies did you use for the frontend and backend, and why?

questions.q: A meeting is created through a REST API call. Participants then need instant updates when someone joins or leaves. Which technology fits best?
o: Updating the DNS record each time someone joins
WebSockets, which keep a two-way connection open for real-time updates
Sending one GET request only when the page first loads
Returning a 304 Not Modified code to every participant
questions.why: REST follows request-response, so the server cannot push updates by itself. WebSockets keep a persistent connection that lets the server push events instantly.
questions.iq: How do the frontend and backend interact when a meeting is created and connected?

questions.q: A user types 'shoes' in a search box, and the frontend calls the backend with a GET request. Where is the search text usually sent?
o: In the DNS lookup for the API domain
In the CSS file linked to the page
In the status code of the request
questions.why: GET requests pass parameters in the URL query string; the backend reads q, searches, and returns matching results as JSON for the frontend to display.
questions.iq: Can you show me in the code what happens when you type a search query, how the API gets called, and how you get the response?

questions.q: A web server must handle many requests at once. Why are threads often preferred over creating a new process for each request?
o: Threads never need locks because they cannot access the same data
Processes cannot handle HTTP requests, only threads can
Threads are cheaper to create and switch, and share memory, though shared data then needs synchronization
Threads are fully isolated, so a crash in one can never affect the others
questions.why: Processes give strong isolation but have higher creation, memory and context-switch costs. Threads are lighter and share memory, which is efficient but introduces race-condition risks.
questions.iq: For a web server handling multiple requests, what are the trade-offs between spinning a new process for each request versus using threads, and why might threads be preferred?

questions.q: App A cannot reach App B at app-b.internal. From A's machine, ping to B's IP address succeeds, but ping to app-b.internal fails with 'could not find host'. What is the most likely cause?
o: B has been assigned the wrong IP address
A firewall is blocking all traffic between the two machines
DNS resolution is misconfigured, so the hostname cannot be turned into an IP
The default gateway on A's machine is wrong
questions.why: A successful ping by IP proves routing, the gateway and basic connectivity work, so the failure is in name resolution. Checking IP, then DNS, then firewall/ports is the standard step-by-step approach.
questions.iq: Two applications running on separate systems are unable to communicate with each other over the network. Explain the step-by-step diagnostic process to troubleshoot this issue, including how misconfigurations in IP addresses, DNS resolution, Firewall rules, or Default Gateways could cause the failure.

questions.q: Which is the correct syntax for an HTML anchor tag that links to Google?
questions.why: An anchor uses <a> with the destination in the href attribute and clickable text between the tags. src is for images, and <link> is not a clickable link.
questions.iq: Write the syntax of an HTML anchor tag.

questions.q: In a React app, what is the main difference between <a> and React Router's <Link>?
o: <Link> reloads the whole page; <a> changes the page without a full reload
<a> reloads the whole page; <Link> changes the page without a full reload
<a> works only for external sites; <Link> works only for images
There is no difference; <Link> is just another name for <a>
questions.why: A plain <a> makes the browser request a new page and reload. <Link> updates the URL and shows the new view inside the same app without a full reload.
questions.iq: What is the difference between `<a>` and `Link`?

questions.q: When should you use an <a> tag instead of a <button>?
o: When clicking should submit a form
When clicking should take the user to another page or URL
When clicking should open a pop-up on the same page
When clicking should run a JavaScript calculation
questions.why: <a> is for navigation to a URL using href. <button> is for actions like submitting a form or running a script.
questions.iq: What is the difference between a <button> and an <a> tag?

questions.q: Which attribute of the <a> tag sets where the link goes?
questions.why: href holds the destination URL. target only controls where it opens (for example, a new tab), and src is used by tags like .
questions.iq: What is the purpose of an anchor (<a>) tag in HTML, and how is it used?

questions.q: In the code below, which are the ATTRIBUTES?
questions.code: About
questions.why: The tag is <a> and "About" is its content. Attributes are the name="value" pairs inside the opening tag: href and target.
questions.iq: What is the difference between a tag and an attribute in HTML?

questions.q: What is the difference between the <link> tag and the <a> tag?
o: <link> creates clickable links in the page; <a> connects CSS files in the <head>
Both create clickable links; <link> is just the newer version
<link> connects resources like CSS in the <head>; <a> creates clickable links in the page
Both load CSS files; <a> is used only for images
questions.why: <link> is a void tag in the <head> that loads resources like stylesheets and is not visible. <a> creates a clickable hyperlink that users see.
questions.iq: What is the difference between the link tag and the anchor tag in HTML?

questions.q: Which task should use the <link> tag rather than the <a> tag?
o: Letting users click to open the Contact page
Opening a PDF file in a new tab
Attaching an external stylesheet to the page
Jumping to a section lower on the same page
questions.why: <link> connects the document to resources like CSS files. Anything the user clicks to go somewhere, even within the same page, uses <a>.
questions.iq: Explain the difference between the link tag and the anchor (a) tag in HTML.

questions.q: What should replace ___ so that clicking the link jumps to the Contact section on the same page?
questions.code:
Go to Contact ...

Contact Us
questions.why: To link within a page, set href to # followed by the target element's id. Without # the browser looks for a file named contact, and .contact is CSS class syntax.
questions.iq: Explain how navigation works within a webpage using HTML. Provide an example of creating an anchor tag for internal navigation.

questions.q: Which statement about common HTML attributes is correct?
o: href on tells the browser which image file to load
class must be unique and used by only one element
id can be shared by many elements on the same page
src on tells the browser which image file to load
questions.why: src gives an image its file path, and href is used on <a> and <link>. id must be unique, while class can be shared.
questions.iq: How do HTML attributes enhance the functionality of elements? Provide examples of commonly used attributes like `id`, `class`, `src`, and `href`.

questions.q: What is the main difference between the id and class attributes?
o: A class should be unique on a page; an id can be shared by many elements
An id should be unique on a page; a class can be shared by many elements
id works only on <div>; class works only on <span>
id adds styling automatically; class adds links automatically
questions.why: An id names one specific element (also used for # links), while a class groups many elements for shared styling. Neither adds styling or links on its own.
questions.iq: How do HTML attributes enhance the functionality of HTML elements? Provide examples of commonly used attributes like `class`, `id`, `src`, and `href`.
